顫音琴屬體鳴樂器，以金屬琴鍵受琴棒敲擊發聲，每鍵下接共鳴管，管內轉動扇葉週期開合: The vibraphone is an idiophone whose metal bars sound when struck by mallets; under each bar is a resonator tube, and a rotating vane inside the tube opens and closes it in cycles, producing a vibrato or tremolo that swells and darkens. When the pedal is up the bars are damped, and when it is pressed the sound sustains for several seconds, so volume and after-ring depend mainly on the pedal and the vanes. The standard range is about three octaves, commonly from the F below middle C to the F above, and there are wider ones. Compared with the glockenspiel and xylophone of the same family, its aluminium bars and deeply arched design make the overtones more harmonious and the timbre softer, and different mallets can give either a bright metallic edge or a round sustained tone.
顫音琴常見於爵士樂，也用於提基酒廊異國風音樂、管弦樂團、管樂隊、行進樂隊前場合奏: The vibraphone is common in jazz, and is also used in the exotic music of tiki lounges, in orchestras, wind bands and the front ensembles of marching bands, and in theatre or film music. Early on it served as a novelty instrument in vaudeville theatre orchestras. The source mentions Lionel Hampton's improvised solo on 'Memories of You', and works such as Alban Berg's 'Lulu' and Leonard Bernstein's 'West Side Story'.
顫音琴為北美體鳴樂器，發聲來自敲擊金屬琴鍵，琴鍵下共鳴管內扇葉由馬達帶動轉動，形: The vibraphone is a North American idiophone; the sound comes from striking the metal bars, and beneath the bars the vanes in the resonator tubes are turned by a motor to make the vibrato, while the pedal controls sustain or damping. A beginner can hold one soft-headed mallet in each hand, strike the bars to get the fixed pitches, then practise pressing and releasing the pedal to control the length of a note. Once that is secure, two mallets in each hand play chords, harmony and arpeggios. In modern works a bow rubbed with rosin can be laid against the short edge of a bar and drawn upwards from the low end, making the bar sound its first overtone.
顫音琴的發聲體為金屬琴鍵，來源載明通常為黃銅或鋁合金，現代琴鍵以鋁材製成。琴鍵下: The vibraphone's sounding body is its metal bars, which the source says are usually brass or aluminium alloy, modern bars being made of aluminium. The resonator tubes below are mostly thin-walled aluminium, though other rigid materials can be used. The frame that carries the bars is built of wooden rails with rubber pads, springs and suspension cord, usually paracord. The mallet heads are rubber balls wrapped in wool or cord, and the shafts are mostly rattan or birch, sometimes fibreglass or nylon. The materials of the vanes, motor and pedal are not stated.

Early instruments had no pedal and steel bars. In 1927 Henry Schluter switched to aluminium bars, adjusted the dimensions and added a damping pedal, which became the modern template. It was first used in vaudeville bands and novelty recordings, and in the 1930s Lionel Hampton's jazz solos turned it towards jazz; early classical works also used it, and it appears in theatre and film music.

The vibraphone (also called vibraharp or vibes) is a percussion instrument of the struck idiophone metal-bar family, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.222, common in the Americas / North America. Its tuned metal bars hang above resonator tubes containing motor-driven metal discs or vanes that turn to open and close the tubes and produce the vibrato; the pedal controls the sustain. The player strikes with mallets, a beginner usually with two and an experienced player often with four, playing chords, harmony and arpeggios, and modern works can also be bowed. It is much used in jazz, in classical solo playing, in orchestras, wind bands and the front ensemble of marching bands, and also appears in theatre or film music.
